newsitem.title: USA: Researchers warn on U.S. encryption access scheme.
newsitem.headline: Researchers warn on U.S. encryption access scheme.

text.p: The U.S. government's plan for gaining access to communications encoded by computers would put at risk the private information and conversations of consumers and businesses, a group of leading cryptography researchers said Wednesday.

Law enforcement and intelligence agencies say they need to be able to crack computer encryption, which scrambles information and renders it unreadable without a software "key," to keep tabs on criminals and spies.
But consumers and businesses are increasingly using the same technology to protect their communications.
For example, encryption is being used to prevent snoopers from intercepting cellular phone calls and to keep hackers from reading credit card numbers sent over the Internet.
The researchers found, however, that the government's plan to crack codes by gaining access to encryption keys would compromise the security of millions of lawful code users.

"The massive deployment of a key recovery infrastructure to meet law enforcement's stated requirements will require significant sacrifices in security and convenience and substantially increased costs to all users of encryption," a study by the researchers concluded.

Although use of encryption within the United States is not directly regulated, the Clinton administration has used export rules and government procurement programmes to encourage development of key recovery systems.

U.S. software companies complain that the export rules hinder their ability to compete with overseas competitors not subject to the restrictions. They want the export rules changed so key recovery is not required for exported products.
On Monday, Sun Microsystems Inc. said it would get around the export rules by selling foreign customers its computer products with encryption made by a Russian company.
A top Clinton official said the researchers had exaggerated the scope of the key recovery system.

"We're not trying to build a giant, Rube Goldberg infrastructure solely to help law enforcement," Under Secretary of Commerce William Reinsch said. "We're trying to help law enforcement append itself to structures the market will build.

But the needs of users and law enforcement agencies may be at odds, the study suggested. "The requirements of government key recovery are almost completely incompatible with those of commercial encryption users," the study said.

Authors of the new report included Matt Blaze, who in 1994 discovered a security flaw in the government's Clipper chip, Jeffrey Schiller, author of the highly-regarded network security programme Kerberos, and Bruce Schneier, inventor of the popular "Blowfish" formula used for encryption.
The full report is available on the Internet at http://www.crypto.com/key_study/.
